prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock alone, as in round 1, and the full exchange has made my reasons more specific rather than changed them. The achievement is a bounded invention with a clear before and after: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or lattice-induced shifts, and Ye's group showed what that idea delivers by reaching systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 and using the many-atom ensemble for new measurements. Independent laboratories reproduce and surpass it, so maturity is not in doubt even though the formal redefinition of the second has not happened; the physics is established whether or not the metrology bodies act this year. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and no other ballot combines that cleanliness with this level of confirmation. I also want to be honest that attribution cleanliness, not a claim that precision metrology is intrinsically deeper than topological phases or a neutrino window, is a large part of why this ranks above its rivals for me.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the lineage honoured in 1997/2001 (laser cooling), 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems); a reader could see the lattice clock as a large improvement in degree. I think the magic-wavelength condition for an ensemble of neutral atoms is a separate concept, but Olsson and Danielsson are right that it cannot be fully dismissed, and it is the reason the citation must name the clock itself. The second objection is that much of its reach (dark matter, varying constants, relativistic geodesy, a new second) is still prospective, and the third is that ion-clock groups, other Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers sit outside the two names. For my own earlier alternatives: B057 has the broadest ranking but its credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D contributors, and the 2016 prize leaves less room; B036 has the conflict I disclose below and sits close to the 2025 prize.

responses.point: B027 overlaps with the 2005 frequency-comb prize, and Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept; B053 aberration correction is a physical object with traceable authorship and a decisive before and after.
responses.response: I accept the first half as a real risk but think it points to the wording, not the names. The concept is Katori's: the magic wavelength is what makes a many-atom neutral clock possible at all, and Ye's contribution is the demonstration that this works at 1e-18 and the use of the ensemble, which I would call development of the clock and not merely tuning. That is why I want 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' in the citation. On B053, I respect the traceable authorship and the maturity, and you were fair in stating that you are the only member who ranked it and are in the field. Where we differ is the criterion: aberration correction is an enabling instrument whose scientific yield appears in other fields, whereas the clock is itself the measurement of nature at a new precision. Given the Krivanek omission and the three-name limit, I do not see it overtaking the clock.

responses.point: B057 is ranked by seven of eight members, combines a clean theory idea (Kane-Mele Z2) with a decisive HgTe experiment, and has fifteen years of confirmation; a prize that does not honour B027 over it needs justification only if B027 is clearly stronger.
responses.response: I take the breadth of ranking seriously, and I agree the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp structure is the natural theory-plus-experiment form, so I keep B057 as my first alternative. But breadth of ranking is not credit, and the omission of Bernevig and Hughes, who proposed HgTe as the platform, is a defect in the science of attribution that a three-name cap cannot cure. A citation built on the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state is defensible, yet it would be contested for years, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. If the committee cannot agree on the clock, B057 is the first thing I would turn to. I do not read your move from B054 as a reason to move myself.

responses.point: B027 is a leading route to the redefinition of the second and has real reach, but its largest scientific payoffs are still mostly prospective, and B041 opens a new observational window that fits the discovery tradition better.
responses.response: I agree that the dark-matter, constants and geodesy payoffs are mostly prospective, and I would not rest the case on them; the case rests on what is already demonstrated, namely reproduced 1e-18 performance and the centimetre-scale time-dilation measurement. On your question of waiting for the redefinition, I would not wait: the achievement does not depend on a committee at the metrology bodies. On B041, I still do not oppose it on science and I have moved it into my alternatives, but Halzen and Karle alone cannot stand for a cubic-kilometre collaboration with an AMANDA predecessor, and I would defer to your astroparticle judgement only if a defensible credit appeared, which I do not see.

responses.point: The citation must be drawn narrowly around the lattice clock itself, since overlap with the 2005 combs prize and the 2012 prize is the strongest argument against and cannot be fully dismissed.
responses.response: We agree, and I would go one step further than my round-1 wording: the citation should say 'optical lattice clock' and should not use 'precision spectroscopy', 'optical clocks' or 'frequency metrology', all of which invite a reading as a repeat of 2005. A tail clause on the 1e-18 level, as you proposed, is useful but not necessary, and I would accept it if it helps the committee see the step as distinct.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the magic-wavelength lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge it so but cannot prove it.
Whether ion-clock groups, other Sr and Yb lattice groups or ultrastable-laser developers have a claim that a two-name credit fails; I accept an attribution cost here.
How the committee should weigh the clean credit of B027 against the broader ranking of B057 if members read the clean credit as a convenience and not as a scientific argument.
I cannot independently verify the detailed division of credit on any ballot beyond the supplied names.
statement.conflict_note: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, with documented ties to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and to co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and I work on circuit and waveguide QED. That is a possible recusal issue for B036 and any related superconducting-circuit candidate, and I would not take part in weighing B036 if it came to a vote; I note that Olsson has flagged Chalmers colleagueship without a specific tie. No connection to B027, Katori or Ye, and none to B057, B041 or the other alternatives, is apparent from my profile. My field, theory of quantum circuits, is neighbouring but distinct from atomic clock physics.
